_readme: Pronunciation system. Each section is shown in English, with only the topic title in Persian. Every row: 'ip' is the big symbol/pattern, 'sub' the secondary reading, 'say' the spoken example (▶ plays it), 'words' extra drilling words, 'note' the caveat. Add a section or a row freely — no code change needed.

blurb.en: Ten vowel sounds carry the whole melody of English. Four pairs change the meaning of a word — say the wrong one and nobody understands you.

tip.en: Persian /a/ splits in two: /æ/ in "bad" (mouth wide, like you are about to say "ah") and /ɑː/ in "car" (mouth relaxed, long). Everything else builds out from there.

name.en: Front vowels — the pairs that trip people up

rows.sub: long vs short, tense vs relaxed
the schwa — see its own section

blurb.en: The most common ending in spoken English. It marks plurals, he/she verbs and possessives — and it has exactly three pronunciations.

tip.en: Never add a vowel after /s/, /z/ or /ʃ/. "buses" is /ˈbjuːzɪz/ — not "busees".

blurb.en: One spelling, three sounds. The rule is purely about the sound before the -ed — learn it and you never guess wrong again.

tip.en: Only /ɪd/ adds a syllable: want → /ˈwɒntɪd/. The other two stay in the same syllable: walked → /wɔːkt/.

name.en: The irregular ones you already know

rows.words: go → went · do → did · make → made
eat → ate · drink → drank · sing → sang
see → saw · take → took · give → gave

blurb.en: Numbers carry money, times and dates. One stressed syllable separates 13 from 30, and one pattern turns 1998 into 'nineteen ninety-eight'.

tip.en: Teens end with a strong -TEEN; tens end with a short -ty. For years, say the first two digits then the last two: 1984 = nineteen eighty-four.

rows.note: the teen ends with a clear /n/; the ten ends in a soft /i/
if the listener hears the wrong one, repeat the whole number slowly
the /t/ in -teen is crisp; -ty is softer and shorter
pair the digits instead of reading every digit
British English keeps 'and'; American English often drops it
both 'twenty ten' and 'two thousand and ten' are heard; stay consistent
write 3/3? British and American readers reverse day and month
o'clock is only for the exact hour
casual speech also says 'four fifty'
the currency word can be dropped after the first mention
American English says 'zero point five'
say each digit after the decimal point
fractions take 'a' or 'one': a quarter

blurb.en: On the phone, spelling is pronunciation. Letters that sound alike, punctuation words and a steady rhythm decide whether your email arrives intact.

tip.en: Spell in small groups and add a clarifying word: 'B as in boy', 'M as in Mike'. Say 'at' and 'dot' clearly; never spell at full speed.

rows.note: for V, the top teeth touch the lower lip; B uses both lips
P has no voice; B buzzes in your throat
M closes the lips; N keeps the mouth open
J starts with /dʒ/, not with the letter G
English letter names do not match Persian vowel names
pause slightly before and after each punctuation word
say 'underscore' for _
say 'double' before the letter, not after it
spell acronyms letter by letter: A-P-I
avoid 'backslash' unless the character really is \
American English says 'zee'; British English says 'zed'

rows.words: B as in boy · C as in cat · D as in dog
F as in Foxtrot · X as in X-ray

rows.note: short groups are easier to copy than one long stream

blurb.en: The stressed syllable is longer, louder and higher. Get it wrong and the word stops being recognised — worse than a wrong consonant.

tip.en: Many nouns and verbs share a spelling but move the beat: ˈRECord (noun) vs reˈCORD (verb). Learn both with their stress marked.

rows.note: the stress moves one syllable right for the verb
two completely different words
the /j/ sound appears in the verb
the /iː/ flips to /ɪ/ in the verb

blurb.en: The most common sound in English — the quiet "uh" in "about". Roughly one syllable in every eight is a schwa. Learn it and your accent starts to sound native.

tip.en: Never stress a schwa — it is by definition unstressed. /bəˈNANə/, never /bəˈNANA/. If a word has two schwas, the stress falls between them.

blurb.en: Nine English sounds with no Persian equivalent. Skip them and no amount of practice will make your accent disappear — they are the last mile.

tip.en: For /θ/ and /ð/ put the tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth and blow — not /s/, not /t/, and never add a vowel after them.

rows.note: the most common mistake is replacing it with /s/
common in: the, that, this, them, there, then

rows.sub: top teeth on the lower lip

rows.note: the tip of the tongue floats; it never curls back

rows.sub: light at the end of a word

blurb.en: Many languages merge /p-b/, /t-d/, /k-g/. English does not — the contrast is how it tells you apart whether you said "cap" or "cab".

tip.en: Put two fingers on your throat. Buzzing = voiced (b, d, g, v, z, j). No buzz = voiceless (p, t, k, f, s, th, sh, ch).

blurb.en: English stacks consonants at the start and end of words. Persian speakers often break the stack with a vowel: 'street' becomes 'estereet', 'asked' becomes 'ask-ed'.

tip.en: Keep the consonants and cut the extra vowel. In 'asked', /k/ and /t/ touch; only /ɪd/ after t or d adds a syllable.

rows.note: no vowel before s; do not say 'estereet'
tongue between the teeth, then straight into /r/
k and t touch; no 'ask-ed'
the plural adds /s/, not a syllable
keep the tongue between the teeth for /θ/

blurb.en: This is the single biggest thing that makes you sound native. Native speakers bury the grammar words and stress only the meaning.

tip.en: Stress nouns, verbs and adjectives. Shrink everything else. "What are you?" is "Wh-re you?", and "I would have gone" is "I would've gone".

rows.words: a lot of · instead of · out of
salt and pepper · fish and chips
have to · going to · used to
I was · we were · you were
for them · tell them · from them
ask for · look for · what for
could have · must have · have to

rows.note: the fastest speakers glue them together
always safe in speech, never in writing
natural even in careful speech
the most natural of all contractions
also: I'd, you'd, he'd

blurb.en: Nobody speaks word by word. English glues words together — this is why native speakers sound fast rather than broken.

tip.en: Three tricks: linking (two consonants join), flapping (t/d between vowels becomes a quick flap), elision (final sounds get dropped).

rows.words: next door · that time · big deal · good day
want to know · need to go · used to be

rows.say: I'll be there in an hour.
rows.words: an honest · a hotel · an hour ago
not at all · what else · how about
put it down · let it go · cut it out
come on in · go on · run on
a lot of time · a lot to do

blurb.en: The melody of the sentence. The same words with a different melody mean something completely different — this is where feeling lives.

tip.en: Do not rise at the end of a statement. A rising "I'm fine." sounds like you are asking, or hiding something.

rows.note: the voice drops and stays down
also surprise, doubt, checking
softens what would sound blunt

rows.say: I want tea, coffee and bread.
rows.note: one fall per item, the last one carries it
the setup lifts, the point drops
the high ending shows it wasn't expected

blurb.en: English spelling does not tell you the sound. A handful of patterns covers most of the exceptions — learn the pattern, not the word.

tip.en: If you read English words aloud, most will be wrong. Read by patterns and sight, not by spelling.

rows.note: there is no rule at all — memorise as a group

rows.words: light · right · high · sight · bright · slight
rows.note: compare with /ɪ/ in think, bring, sing
the most irregular vowel spelling in English

rows.words: know · write · answer · half · calm · island · Wednesday

rows.sub: a silent e makes the vowel long

blurb.en: Stress is not volume. Moving the beat to a different word changes what you deny, correct or compare — the same sentence can answer four different misunderstandings.

tip.en: Put one strong beat on the word you are contrasting, then let the rest fall. Do not stress every word; that sounds angry, not clear.

rows.ip: I didn't say he stole it.
rows.say: I didn't say he stole it.
rows.note: stress: I

rows.ip: I didn't say he stole it.
rows.say: I didn't say he stole it.
rows.note: stress: say

rows.ip: I didn't say he stole it.
rows.say: I didn't say he stole it.
rows.note: stress: he

rows.ip: I didn't say he stole it.
rows.say: I didn't say he stole it.
rows.note: stress: stole

rows.say: Actually, I think we need more time.
rows.note: stress 'think', then fall on 'more time'
fall on the correct fact, not on 'not'

rows.say: I see your point, but the cost is too high.
rows.note: two beats: 'point' and 'too high'
stress both numbers for the contrast
repeat the name, then spell it
the contrast carries the correction

blurb.en: English is a stress-timed language: the important words land on the beat and everything else gets crushed between them. Get this right and people will call you 'natural' before you finish the sentence.

tip.en: One main stress per information group. Say the group, pause, say the next one. Never put equal weight on every word.

rows.say: I bought a new car last week.
rows.note: function words ride in between, unstressed

rows.sub: when a word becomes the verb
rows.words: light·to light · second·a second · present·to present

rows.say: I'd like to book a table for two.
When I arrived, the meeting had already started.
I would really like to help you.
Reading fluently is a matter of practice.
Well, I mean, it depends, doesn't it?
That's a good idea. But it needs work.

blurb.en: Presenting, selling, persuading — the melody does as much work as the words. These patterns make you sound prepared rather than merely correct.

tip.en: Slow down and drop your pitch on the words that matter. Speed and rising pitch signal nervousness, not confidence.

rows.say: Revenue rose by forty per cent.
That is where we are today.
We can deliver this by Friday.
That won't work for the team.
We have a new offer on the table.
I understand, but I see it differently.

blurb.en: At native speed, unstressed syllables lose their vowels entirely. If you pronounce every syllable you will sound slow — and slightly foreign, however good your accent is.

tip.en: Syllables you never stress never keep a full vowel. "Every" is two beats, but "everywhere" is closer to two and a half.
